section.title: Overview
section.para: This module provides a DB APIv1 connector that carries database operations over NATS request/reply instead of talking to a database server directly. A backend service subscribed to the configured subjects executes the operations and replies.
Because it implements the generic &kamailio; database interface, any module that takes a db_url can use it - usrloc, auth_db, permissions, htable, dialog and so on.
A reference backend implementation in Go, which executes the requests against MySQL, is shipped in misc/external/db_nats/.

Operations are sent as structured, typed JSON and the backend binds the values as query parameters. Values are therefore never concatenated into SQL. This differs from a driver such as db_mysql, which quotes values locally with mysql_real_escape_string(); db_nats has no local database connection and so cannot escape safely on its own.

listitem.para: No transactions. START TRANSACTION, COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT, SET AUTOCOMMIT, SET SESSION, LOCK TABLES, GET_LOCK() and SELECT ... FOR UPDATE all require a connection that persists across calls. Over stateless request/reply each statement may reach a different backend and a different database connection. See the session_sql_mode parameter.
No LAST_INSERT_ID, INSERT DELAYED or async queries. These entry points are not implemented. Every module in the tree null-tests them, so nothing breaks by their absence.
Every operation blocks the calling process until the reply arrives or request_timeout expires. With usrloc db_mode=3 this puts a round trip on every lookup and save.

Some modules load an entire table in a single query with no fetch fallback (for example permissions). The NATS max_payload must be large enough for those replies. Modules that honour DB_CAP_FETCH, such as usrloc, page through a server-side cursor instead and are not affected.

section.title: Dependencies
section.para: The NATS C client library (nats.c, version 2.0 or later) must be installed. Unlike the nats module, db_nats does not need libuv: it uses synchronous request/reply rather than an event loop.

section.title: Database URL
section.para: The URL gives the NATS server and the subject namespace:
The path selects the subject prefix; when omitted, the subject_prefix parameter is used. Three subjects are derived from it:
They are separate so that NATS account permissions can deny the raw subject for a given credential, keeping enforcement on the bus.

section.title: nats_url (string)
section.para: A NATS server to connect to. May be set several times to give a cluster, up to 10 entries, in the same style as the nats module.

The srdb1 database URL cannot express a server list: a comma in db_url is not parsed as a separator but scattered across the host, password and database fields, which would silently connect to the wrong place. db_nats therefore refuses any db_url containing a comma and expects the cluster here instead.
When at least one nats_url is set, the host in db_url is ignored entirely and only its path is used, to select the subject prefix. Give it a placeholder host in that case.
Credentials may be embedded per server. They are masked in log output.

example.title: A cluster with credentials
example.programlisting:
modparam("db_nats", "nats_url", "nats://user:pass@10.0.0.1:4222") modparam("db_nats", "nats_url", "nats://user:pass@10.0.0.2:4222") modparam("db_nats", "nats_url", "nats://user:pass@10.0.0.3:4222")
# host is a placeholder here; only the path is used modparam("usrloc", "db_url", "nats://cluster/kamailio.db")

section.title: request_timeout (int)
section.para: How long to wait for a reply, in milliseconds. The calling process is blocked for this period, so on a SIP worker it is a stall budget: keep it well below your transaction timers.

section.title: connect_timeout (int)
section.para: Connection establishment timeout, in milliseconds.

section.title: error_penalty (int)
section.para: After a transport error, fail subsequent requests immediately for this many milliseconds instead of attempting them. Set to 0 to disable.

Without it, every query during an outage waits out request_timeout, and each one blocks the calling process for that long. With it, one request per window probes the connection and the rest fail at once.

Note this state is per process: the connection lives in private memory and is keyed by pid, so each worker keeps its own window. The cost of an outage is therefore roughly one timeout per window per process, not one globally.

section.title: error_threshold (int)
section.para: How many consecutive transport errors a process must see before it opens an error_penalty window. Raise it to tolerate isolated blips at the cost of more requests waiting out the full timeout.

section.title: session_sql_mode (string)
section.para: What to do when a raw query carries session state (COMMIT, SET AUTOCOMMIT, LOCK TABLES and similar). Either reject or ignore.

listitem.para: reject - the call fails with an error.
ignore - the call succeeds as a no-op and a warning is logged. Use this only when the caller can tolerate losing atomicity and isolation.

section.para: In both cases the statement is never sent. There is deliberately no forwarding mode: a forwarded SET AUTOCOMMIT=0 would leave a pooled backend connection with autocommit disabled for every later unrelated query, while the matching COMMIT reached a different connection.

section.title: subject_prefix (string)
section.para: Subject prefix used when the database URL has no path.

section.title: max_reconnect (int)
section.para: Maximum reconnect attempts made by the NATS client.

section.title: reconnect_wait (int)
section.para: Delay between reconnect attempts, in milliseconds.

section.title: Result size and private memory
section.para: Replies are parsed into private (pkg) memory, and a JSON document costs considerably more than its wire size once parsed into nodes and copied into result values. Budget roughly 40 to 50 times the reply size in pkg memory.

This matters for modules that page through large tables. With usrloc's default fetch_rows of 2000, a page of the location table is around 450 kB on the wire and needs about 24 MB of pkg to decode - more than the 8 MB default. The symptom is a failed to parse reply json error during preload.
Either lower fetch_rows (500 works comfortably within the default pkg for the location table) or raise pkg memory with the -M command line option.

Separately, a reply must fit the NATS server's max_payload, 1 MB by default. Modules that page through a cursor are naturally bounded by their fetch size. Modules that load a whole table in one query and have no fetch fallback, such as permissions, are not: for those the backend answers with a reply_too_large error rather than leaving the request to time out, and max_payload must be raised or the query narrowed.

section.title: Running more than one backend
section.para: Backends subscribe as a queue group, so ordinary operations are spread across every instance. Cursors are the exception: an open cursor holds a live result set inside one backend process and cannot be served by another. The reply that opens a cursor therefore carries a cursor_subject naming its owner, and db_nats addresses all continuation there rather than to the shared subject.

A backend that does not send cursor_subject still works, but only when a single instance is running: with more than one, fetches are load balanced away from the cursor's owner and fail with a message saying the cursor is no longer available.

If the owning instance stops, an open cursor is lost. The fetch fails promptly rather than hanging, and the operation in progress - a usrloc preload, for example - is reported as failed. db_nats deliberately does not reopen the query behind the caller's back, since restarting a partly consumed result would silently skip or duplicate rows.

A backend being restarted deliberately does not have this effect: on SIGTERM it stops accepting new work but keeps serving already-open cursors until they finish or its grace period expires, so a preload in progress completes rather than failing.

One queue group must serve exactly one logical database. Operations are load balanced, so backends in the same group pointing at different databases would answer the same query from different data, non-deterministically. Give each database its own subject prefix, selected per module through the path of db_url. Read replicas of one database are equally unsuitable, because a cursor is bound to a single connection's snapshot.

section.title: Module compatibility
section.para: Two modules drive SQL transactions through raw queries and cannot work correctly without connection affinity: ims_usrloc_scscf and p_usrloc. Note that p_usrloc's failover path is not gated by its db_use_transactions parameter, so disabling that is not sufficient.

At startup db_nats inspects those modules' configured database URLs. If one of them actually points at db_nats, startup fails with an explanatory error when session_sql_mode is reject, or logs a warning when it is ignore. A module pointed at a different driver is left alone.
sqlops requires DB_CAP_RAW_QUERY at startup, so the raw subject must be reachable and the backend must permit raw statements for it to work.

section.title: Backend contract
section.para: Two encoding rules matter when writing your own backend:

listitem.para: Every value travels as a JSON string, never a JSON number. The module parses replies with srjson, which stores all numbers as double, so a 64-bit integer sent as a number would be silently corrupted above 2^53.
Values of type datetime are unix epoch seconds in both directions.

section.para: Column types must be reported accurately. In particular text columns must be declared string and not str, because only the former is NUL-terminated when copied, and modules such as usrloc and auth_db read values with VAL_STRING() and strlen(). A SQL NULL is sent as a JSON null in the row array.
The backend must also serve the version table with an integer version column, since most modules call db_check_table_version() at startup.
